title: The Gifts and the Spiral: Wright, the Valley, and the Two Fires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Richland Center, the birth on the Pine River
stops.date_confidence: birth date 8 June 1867 attested (Wikipedia infobox; Secrest, Frank Lloyd Wright: A Biography, 1992). Wright himself claimed 1869 throughout much of his life; the gathering pass filed that as legend, and the verification pass corrected it to attested biographical fact, a documented self-backdating. The pin is the town: the birth house is demolished.
stops.campa: On the eighth of June a son is born at Richland Center, Wisconsin, to William Cary Wright, a preacher and music teacher who moves his family wherever a pulpit calls, and to Anna Lloyd Jones, of the Welsh farming clan settled in a valley two counties east. The house is later pulled down, so the town has to stand in for the room. For most of his adult life he will tell people he was born in 1869, shaving two years off a life that ends up needing none of the help.
suggested_refs: The demolished Wright birth house at Richland Center, Wisconsin
sources: Meryle Secrest, Frank Lloyd Wright: A Biography (1992)

stops.name: Weymouth, the parsonage years
stops.date_confidence: the pool's geography entry gives 1876-1878 for the Weymouth residence; its own verification pass corrects the move to 1874, with a return to Wisconsin c. 1877-78 after financial hardship (Wikipedia). Both readings are recorded and 1874 is used. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: William Cary Wright takes the pulpit of the First Congregational church at Weymouth, Massachusetts, and the family follows him east into the parsonage. Anna keeps a house on a preacher's income that never quite covers it, and within three years the money runs out and they turn back toward Wisconsin. The boy is between seven and ten in these years. Eighty years later, at eighty-eight, he is asked by a New York reporter what ought to be done about Boston.
stops.quote: Clear out 800,000 people and preserve it as a museum piece.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright on Boston, quoted in The New York Times, 27 November 1955
suggested_refs: The First Congregational Church parsonage at Weymouth, Massachusetts
sources: Frank Lloyd Wright, An Autobiography (1932, 1943 ed.)

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Centennial and the Gifts
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 1876 Froebel Gifts in the Wright household are attested (Wikipedia). The claim that Anna encountered the system AT the Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition rests solely on Wright's An Autobiography (1932/1943); Wikipedia carries the Gifts without the Centennial. The gathering pass tagged this attested twice, the verification pass demoted both to reconstruction as retrospective self-mythology, and the demotion is accepted. Month set to June as a convention.
stops.campa: At the Centennial Exhibition in Fairmount Park, among the machines and the pavilions of a hundred nations, a display of Friedrich Froebel's kindergarten Gifts is set out: maple spheres, cylinders and cubes, and the gridded tables they are laid upon. Anna Lloyd Wright, a teacher, carries the system home to her nine-year-old. This is the story Wright tells in 1932, fifty-six years after the fact, and no source but his own carries it. It is recorded here as a story he told, not as an established fact.
suggested_refs: Froebel's Gifts and Occupations as exhibited in the American kindergarten displays of the 1870s
Norman Brosterman, Inventing Kindergarten
sources: Richard MacCormac, 'Froebel's Kindergarten Gifts and the Early Architectural Education of Frank Lloyd Wright'

stops.name: Madison, the house on East Gorham Street
stops.date_confidence: residence attested 1878-1885 (Secrest; An Autobiography). Coordinate corrected: the pool's 43.0731/-89.3812 falls south of the Capitol on the Lake Monona side, while East Gorham Street runs north along Mendota; re-pinned near 43.0806/-89.3781. Separation 1881, filing 1884, divorce granted 1885, all attested (Wikipedia). Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The family comes back to Wisconsin and settles on East Gorham Street in Madison, on the Lake Mendota side of the isthmus, a few blocks from the Capitol. The boy is put to school. His parents are already coming apart: they separate the year he turns fourteen, his father files in 1884, and when the divorce is granted in 1885 William Cary Wright leaves the state and never sees his son again. The Lloyd Joneses close around the household, and from here on the mother's family is the only family there is.
suggested_refs: The Wright family house on East Gorham Street, Madison
Madison High School, attended 1885

stops.name: Spring Green, the summers in the Valley
stops.date_confidence: the boyhood summers are attested to the 1878-1885 span (An Autobiography; Secrest) but no source reached names the year they began or which farm; 1880 and the month are conventional. GAP declared. Pinned at the later Taliesin coordinate 43.1411/-90.0706 as a stand-in for the Valley, correcting the pool's 43.1489/-90.0729, which is about 900 m north.
stops.campa: Every summer from about eleven he is sent down to the Lloyd Jones farms in the valley near Spring Green to work for his uncle James until his hands are ruined and his opinion of farm labor is fixed for life. The family calls the place the Valley. It has a chapel, a school his aunts will run, and hillsides his mother's people have farmed since they came over from Wales. He will buy into it, build on it, burn out of it twice, bury his dead in it, and be dug out of it himself twenty-six years after he is put in.
stops.quote: Study nature, love nature, stay close to nature. It will never fail you.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright, cited to The Wright Style (1992), a secondary compilation; the underlying Wright text was not located
suggested_refs: The Lloyd Jones farms and Unity Chapel in the valley near Spring Green, Wisconsin

stops.name: Madison, Science Hall and the degree he does not take
stops.date_confidence: admission 1886 and departure for Chicago 1887 (Wikipedia). The pool's geography entry gives the span as 1885-1887 and contradicts its own chronology, which gives 1886; both are recorded and 1886 is used. Coordinate 43.0761/-89.4022 is Science Hall; the pool's 43.0757/-89.4001 is about 180 m off and would also have served. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is admitted to the University of Wisconsin as a special student and reads civil engineering under Allan D. Conover. He never takes a degree. What he keeps from the year is a set of hands that know how a load travels through a structure, which is not what the Beaux-Arts academies teach. By 1887 he has gone to Chicago, where the fire of sixteen years before has left a city still rebuilding itself, and where a young man who can draw can be paid for it inside a week.
suggested_refs: Science Hall, University of Wisconsin-Madison, and the engineering teaching of Allan D. Conover

stops.name: Chicago, the first drafting board
stops.date_confidence: employment with Silsbee in 1887 attested (Wikipedia). The tradition that Silsbee had designed the Lloyd Jones chapel and that this is why Wright went to him is tagged as reconstruction in the pool and stays there. Coordinate is the canonical Chicago pin 41.8781/-87.6298, inherited byte-identical from l_frank_baum.journey.json, which cites it as already shared with maurice_sendak, otto_hanish and fyodor_yevtishchev; the pool's own 41.8825/-87.6285 is not used. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He finds work as a draftsman for Joseph Lyman Silsbee, who is putting up All Souls Church and turning out shingle-style houses fast enough to keep several boards busy. Family tradition holds that Silsbee had designed the Lloyd Jones chapel back in the Valley, and that this is why Wright goes to him first; nothing firmer than tradition supports it. The wage is modest and the drawing is picturesque. Within the year he leaves it for Adler and Sullivan.
suggested_refs: Joseph Lyman Silsbee's All Souls Church, Chicago
The Lloyd Jones family chapel in the Wisconsin valley, attributed to Silsbee

stops.name: Chicago, Adler and Sullivan
stops.date_confidence: Wright joined Adler and Sullivan around November 1887 (Wikipedia); the pool's geography entry gives 1888-1893 and is corrected. Pinned at the Auditorium Building 41.8757/-87.6257, but the firm did not occupy its tower offices there until 1890, the building having been completed in December 1889, so the first years were worked elsewhere. Head draftsman by 1890 with George Elmslie, attested. The Sullivan loan for the Oak Park house is standard in the biographies and is not separately attested in the verified pool.
stops.campa: He joins Adler and Sullivan, the firm turning the tall office building into a form rather than a stack, and works directly under Louis Sullivan, whom he will call Lieber Meister for the rest of his life and never quite forgive. By 1890 he is head draftsman, sharing an office with George Elmslie, and the firm has moved into the tower of its own Auditorium Building. Sullivan lends him the money for the Oak Park house. The loan is in all the biographies; the verified record does not carry it.
suggested_refs: The Auditorium Building tower offices of Adler and Sullivan, occupied from 1890
The Sullivan-Wright correspondence cited in Secrest

stops.name: Oak Park, the house for Catherine Tobin
stops.date_confidence: marriage and house both 1889, attested (Wikipedia; Frank Lloyd Wright Trust). Coordinate corrected to 41.8942/-87.7997, 428 Forest Avenue and 951 Chicago Avenue; the pool's 41.8917/-87.7967 is about 370 m south-east. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He marries Catherine Tobin, called Kitty, and builds them a house at Forest and Chicago Avenues in Oak Park, a village of churches west of the city. He is twenty-two and has been in Chicago two years, and he designs it while still on Sullivan's payroll. Six children will be born in the house. It is a shingled thing under a great triangular gable, and he keeps altering it for twenty years as the children come. What he settles on his own walls he sells to the neighbours inside a decade.
suggested_refs: The Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio, 428 Forest Avenue, Oak Park
sources: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust, Home and Studio documentation

stops.name: Chicago, the bootlegged houses and the Schiller Building
stops.date_confidence: the bootlegged houses, the break with Sullivan and the Schiller Building office are all attested to 1893 (Wikipedia); no month is given. Baum's residence beside the White City and the biographers' Emerald City connection are attested in l_frank_baum.journey.json, which does not name Wright. The claim circulating in the queue notes that Wright helped design fair pavilions for Sullivan is not attested in any source reached and is not made here. Canonical Chicago pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Sullivan finds out that his head draftsman has been designing houses on the side against the terms of his contract, and the two men part after a quarrel neither will afterward describe the same way twice. Wright opens his own office in the Schiller Building. It is the year of the Columbian Exposition, and the White City stands in plaster along the lakefront, a classical dream he will spend forty years arguing against. L. Frank Baum is living beside it, taking notes for a city made of a different material.
stops.quote: Early in life I had to choose between honest arrogance and hypocritical humility. I chose honest arrogance and have seen no occasion to change.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright; cited on Wikiquote to The World's Best Thoughts on Life and Living (1981, comp. Eugene Raudsepp) and to The Michigan Daily, 10 November 1998
suggested_refs: The Schiller Building, Chicago, first office of Wright's independent practice
The World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 and its White City

stops.name: River Forest, the Winslow House
stops.date_confidence: the Winslow House completed 1894, the Steinway Hall move 1896, and the Marion Mahony collaboration are all attested (Wikipedia); no months are given. GAP: the verified pool carries no coordinate for the Winslow House, so the pin is the River Forest municipal centroid rather than the building. Steinway Hall is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: In River Forest, next door to Oak Park, he builds the William H. Winslow house: a low hipped roof with wide eaves, a banded brick base, an ornamented frieze under the overhang, and a front so symmetrical and so calm that Winslow's neighbours are said to have laughed at him for it. It is the first house that is fully Wright's and not Sullivan's. Two years later he moves the practice into Steinway Hall, sharing a floor and the talk with the men who will be called the Prairie School, Marion Mahony among them.
suggested_refs: The William H. Winslow House, Auvergne Place, River Forest, Illinois
Steinway Hall, Chicago, and the Prairie School draughtsmen who shared it

stops.name: Oak Park, the studio added to the house
stops.date_confidence: the studio addition was completed February 1898 (Frank Lloyd Wright Trust); day defaulted. The two Ladies' Home Journal articles are attested to 1901 (Wikipedia) and are folded into this stop rather than given their own. Coordinate corrected as at the 1889 stop.
stops.campa: He adds a studio to the Oak Park house: an octagonal drafting room hung from chains, a library, a barrel-vaulted playroom for the children, and a door to the street so clients need not walk through the kitchen. Work and household are now one building. Within three years he publishes A Home in a Prairie Town and A Small House with Lots of Room in It in the Ladies' Home Journal, putting the new house type in front of a million subscribers before he has built fifty of them.
suggested_refs: The 1898 studio addition to the Oak Park house
'A Home in a Prairie Town' and 'A Small House with Lots of Room in It', Ladies' Home Journal, 1901
sources: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust, Home and Studio documentation

stops.name: Spring Green, the Hillside Home School for the aunts
stops.date_confidence: designed and built 1902-1907 (Taliesin Preservation documentation); month and day defaulted. Coordinate 43.1417/-90.0781 as given in the pool, distinct from Taliesin proper at 43.1411/-90.0706, the two sites lying a short distance apart in the same valley.
stops.campa: Back in the Valley he builds a school for his aunts Nell and Jane Lloyd Jones, who have been running a coeducational boarding school on the family land since before he left for Chicago. Sandstone quarried out of the hill, oak from the woodlot, an assembly room with a gallery over it. The commission keeps him tied to Spring Green through the whole Oak Park decade, and it puts his own building on the ground he will move back to. Thirty years later the same rooms will house his apprentices.
suggested_refs: The Hillside Home School building, Spring Green, built for Nell and Jane Lloyd Jones

stops.name: Buffalo, the Darwin D. Martin House
stops.date_confidence: designed and built 1903-1905 (Martin House Restoration Corporation); the pool's chronology gives completion in 1904 while its geography gives 1903-1905, and both are recorded. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate 42.9284/-78.8567 as given, uncorrected. That Martin financed Wright for decades is standard in the literature and is not itemised in the verified pool.
stops.campa: Darwin D. Martin, an executive of the Larkin Soap Company in Buffalo, commissions a house in 1903 and gets an estate: a main house, a pergola running the length of the lot to a conservatory, a carriage house, a gardener's cottage, and a second house for his sister, all strung on one long axis with brick piers and art glass by the acre. Building runs to 1905. Martin becomes the patron who lends Wright money for the next thirty years and is never fully repaid.
suggested_refs: The Darwin D. Martin House complex, 125 Jewett Parkway, Buffalo

stops.name: Buffalo, the Larkin Administration Building
stops.date_confidence: designed January 1903 to April 1904, built 1904, opened late 1906, demolished February to July 1950 (Wikipedia, 'Larkin Administration Building'). The pool's chronology, which has Wright designing it in 1905, contradicts its own geography span of 1904-1906 and is not used. Coordinate corrected by about 1.7 km to 42.8772/-78.8519, 680 Seneca Street. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: For the Larkin Soap Company he builds an office block on Seneca Street with its windows turned inward: a sealed brick shell, stair towers pulled clear at the corners, a top-lit central court five storeys deep, air washed and tempered before it is delivered to the clerks, and steel furniture bolted to the floor so that nobody can rearrange it. It is designed between 1903 and 1904 and opens late in 1906. Buffalo pulls it down in 1950 and puts a truck lot on the site.
suggested_refs: The Larkin Administration Building, 680 Seneca Street, Buffalo, demolished 1950
sources: Larkin Company archives, cited in Secrest (1992)

stops.name: Oak Park, Unity Temple in poured concrete
stops.date_confidence: designed 1905, built to 1908, dedicated September 1909 (Frank Lloyd Wright Trust). The pool's chronology entry claiming the building was completed in 1905 contradicts its own geography span of 1905-1908 and is not used; the stop is dated to the design year, month and day defaulted. The remark about becoming an architect of space is attributed to Wright in the pool without a located primary text, which is recorded as a gap.
stops.campa: His own Unitarian congregation in Oak Park loses its church to fire and cannot afford stone. He gives them poured concrete, left unfaced because facing costs money, in two blocks joined by a low entrance: the temple for worship, the house for everything else. Inside, light falls from a coffered ceiling onto a room where nobody sits more than a few rows from the pulpit. He says later that this is where he stopped being an architect of structure and became an architect of space.
stops.quote: The soul of any civilization on earth has ever been and still is Art and Religion.
suggested_refs: Unity Temple, 875 Lake Street, Oak Park, dedicated September 1909
sources: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust, Unity Temple documentation

stops.name: Chicago, the Robie House
stops.date_confidence: designed 1908, built 1909-1910 (Frank Lloyd Wright Trust); the stop is dated to the design year, month and day defaulted. Fermi's Hyde Park and University of Chicago stops are attested in fermi.journey.json, which makes no Wright reference; the proximity here is geographic and is asserted as nothing more.
stops.campa: On a narrow corner lot in Hyde Park he builds, for Frederick C. Robie, a bicycle and motor parts man of twenty-eight, a house with a roof cantilevered out past any visible support, a continuous band of art glass, a chimney mass the whole plan turns around, and no elevation that reads as a front. Thirty-four years later, a few blocks off under the Stagg Field stands, Enrico Fermi will stack graphite and uranium in the same neighbourhood and start a chain reaction.
suggested_refs: The Frederick C. Robie House, 5757 South Woodlawn Avenue, Chicago
sources: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust, Robie House documentation

stops.name: Berlin, the Wasmuth Portfolio
stops.date_confidence: Wright in Berlin on the Wasmuth work in 1910 (Secrest; Alofsin, Frank Lloyd Wright: The Lost Years); the pool's chronology dates the portfolio's publication to 1911. Both dates are carried and the stop is set at 1910, month and day defaulted. Coordinate 52.51/13.39 as given.
stops.campa: He has left his wife and six children and gone to Europe with Mamah Borthwick Cheney, a client's wife. In Berlin he works with the publisher Ernst Wasmuth on a folio of lithographed plates of his own buildings, drawn and redrawn for the purpose. It reaches architects in Germany and the Netherlands who have never seen an American house that was not a copy of a European one. Oak Park reads about the affair in the newspapers, and the practice there does not survive the reading.
suggested_refs: Ausgefuhrte Bauten und Entwurfe von Frank Lloyd Wright, Ernst Wasmuth Verlag, Berlin
sources: Anthony Alofsin, Frank Lloyd Wright: The Lost Years

stops.name: Fiesole, the year above Florence
stops.date_confidence: the Fiesole residence in 1910 is attested (Alofsin; Secrest) and the coordinate 43.8064/11.2925 is sound. The villa name is flagged as unverified: the pool's 'Villa Fortuna' is judged invented or garbled by its own verification pass, which gives Villino Belvedere on Via Verdi from the Wright literature. Borthwick's months in Germany and Sweden pursuing her divorce are recorded in Wikipedia, 'Mamah Borthwick'. Month set to June as a convention.
stops.campa: Above Florence, at Fiesole, he and Mamah Borthwick take a small villa and work: he on the Wasmuth drawings, she on translations of Ellen Key. One source names the house Villa Fortuna; the Wright literature calls it the Villino Belvedere on Via Verdi, and the name is left unresolved rather than guessed at. Nor are they there the whole year. She spends part of 1910 in Germany and Sweden, pursuing a divorce Edwin Cheney has not yet agreed to grant her.
suggested_refs: The Fiesole residence of 1910, named Villino Belvedere in the Wright literature
Mamah Borthwick's translations of Ellen Key

stops.name: Spring Green, Taliesin raised on the shining brow
stops.date_confidence: land purchased by Anna Lloyd Jones Wright and construction begun in May 1911 (Wikipedia; Taliesin Preservation); day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to 43.1411/-90.0706, 5607 County Road C; the pool's 43.1478/-90.0725 is about 750 m north, an error it repeats at four separate entries and which is corrected at all four.
stops.campa: His mother buys the hillside below the Lloyd Jones chapel and he begins building on it in May: limestone laid in courses like the outcrop it came out of, plaster the colour of the sand, a house that stops below the crown of the hill instead of crossing it. He calls it Taliesin, after the Welsh bard, shining brow. It is a house for a man and a woman who cannot be married in the state of Wisconsin, set down in the middle of the only people left anywhere who will have them.
stops.quote: No house should ever be on a hill or on anything. It should be of the hill. Belonging to it.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright, An Autobiography (1932), p. 168
suggested_refs: Taliesin, 5607 County Road C, Spring Green, Wisconsin

stops.name: Chicago, Midway Gardens
stops.date_confidence: designed and built 1913-1914 and demolished during Prohibition (Secrest); no month is reached for the opening, and the demolition year is given only loosely in the pool, so no year is stated for it here. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate 41.7853/-87.6033 at Sixtieth Street and Cottage Grove, as given.
stops.campa: Back in Chicago he builds Midway Gardens at Sixtieth and Cottage Grove: a concert garden and beer hall of brick and patterned cast concrete, with sprites and abstract murals he designs himself, an orchestra shell, and terraces stepping down into an open court. It opens in the summer of 1914. Prohibition kills the business that pays for it, and the building is demolished before it is twenty years old. Almost nothing survives except the photographs and a handful of the sprites.
suggested_refs: Midway Gardens, Sixtieth Street and Cottage Grove, Chicago, demolished

stops.name: Spring Green, the fifteenth of August
stops.date_confidence: 15 August 1914 attested (Weekly Home News, Spring Green, August 1914, via Secrest; Wikipedia). The weapon is contradicted: both pool entries say axe, while the verification pass gives a roofing hatchet or shingling tool per Wikipedia, 'Mamah Borthwick'; the hatchet is used here and the divergence is recorded. Seven dead is confirmed; the composition of the seven beyond Borthwick and her two children comes from the standard accounts and is not itemised in the verified pool. Coordinate corrected as above.
stops.campa: Wright is in Chicago finishing Midway Gardens. At Taliesin the servant Julian Carlton serves lunch, locks the doors of the living quarters, sets the place alight, and kills the people coming out of it with a hatchet. Seven die, among them Mamah Borthwick and her two children. Wright comes back on the night train, buries her himself in the Lloyd Jones ground beside the chapel, and cuts flowers from the garden to fill the coffin. He rebuilds on the same stone within the year.
suggested_refs: Contemporary press accounts of the Taliesin murders, Weekly Home News (Spring Green), August 1914
Mamah Borthwick's grave in the Lloyd Jones family cemetery

segments.name: Tokyo, the Desert Blocks, the Second Fire

stops.name: Tokyo, the Imperial Hotel commission
stops.date_confidence: the pool contradicts itself three ways on the Japan dating: chronology says the work begins 1917, geography gives 1913-1923, and the verification pass gives a first visit in 1905, the commission in 1916, and residence supervising construction 1917-1922. All three readings are recorded; the stop is dated to the commission year, month and day defaulted. Coordinate 35.6733/139.7592, Uchisaiwaicho. The print dealing as a source of income is standard in the literature and is not attested in the verified pool.
stops.campa: The Imperial Hotel commission reaches him and he takes it: a low sprawling building of oya stone and brick on soft Tokyo ground, floated on short piles driven into the mud like a ship at anchor rather than founded on rock. He is resident in Tokyo through most of the construction, some five years of it, with pools in the forecourt that are there to be pretty and also to hold water. He had first come to Japan in 1905, buying prints. The print dealing keeps him in money for twenty years, on the biographers' word rather than the record's.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Hotel, Uchisaiwaicho, Tokyo, and its floating foundation
sources: Kathryn Smith, Frank Lloyd Wright and the Imperial Hotel

stops.name: Los Angeles, Hollyhock House on Olive Hill
stops.date_confidence: designed and built 1919-1921 (City of Los Angeles, Hollyhock House / Barnsdall Art Park documentation); month and day defaulted. The delegation of site supervision to Rudolph Schindler and Lloyd Wright, and Barnsdall's later gift of the property to the city, are standard in the institutional literature and are not separately attested in the verified pool. Coordinate 34.1017/-118.2872 as given.
stops.campa: The oil heiress Aline Barnsdall buys an olive-planted hill in East Hollywood and asks for a theatre, houses, and a residence on top of it. Wright gives her a heavy stucco mass with battered walls and an abstracted hollyhock cut into cast stone all round it, a courtyard house facing inward, with a moat and a roof pool. He is in Japan for most of the building and leaves the site to Rudolph Schindler and to his son Lloyd. Barnsdall gives the house away to the city not long after moving in.
suggested_refs: Hollyhock House, Olive Hill, Barnsdall Art Park, Los Angeles
sources: City of Los Angeles, Hollyhock House / Barnsdall Art Park documentation

stops.name: Pasadena, La Miniatura and the textile block
stops.date_confidence: 1923, first of the four textile-block houses, confirmed (Frank Lloyd Wright Trust; Wikipedia). Two corrections to the pool: the coordinate is 34.1554/-118.1618 at 645 Prospect Crescent, about 850 m from the pin given, and the entry filed the house under Los Angeles when Pasadena is a separate incorporated city. That the house leaked is standard in the literature and is not attested in the verified pool. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: In a ravine in Pasadena he builds La Miniatura for the rare book dealer Alice Millard: concrete blocks cast on site, patterned and perforated, threaded together with steel rods so that the wall is knitted rather than laid. He calls the system textile block, and he means it as a way of making a cheap material into an architecture. It is the first of four in southern California. The biographers say it leaked from the start; the verified record does not carry that. Three more follow within two years.
suggested_refs: The Alice Millard House, La Miniatura, 645 Prospect Crescent, Pasadena

stops.name: Tokyo, the hotel and the earthquake
stops.date_confidence: the hotel was completed 1923, survived the Great Kanto Earthquake of the same year, and was demolished in 1968 (Wikipedia; Kathryn Smith). The earthquake date of 1 September 1923 is general record. The transmission of the news to the American press, and the later engineering argument over how much of the survival was the design, are standard in the literature and are not attested in the verified pool.
stops.campa: On the first of September the Great Kanto earthquake levels Yokohama and burns most of Tokyo. The Imperial Hotel, finished that year, comes through it standing, and the news goes round the American press within days as proof of the floating foundation. Engineers will argue for decades about how much of the survival was the design and how much was the fireproofing and luck. The building stands until 1968, when it is pulled down to make room for a taller one.
suggested_refs: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 and the survival of the Imperial Hotel
sources: Kathryn Smith, Frank Lloyd Wright and the Imperial Hotel

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Ennis House on the ridge
stops.date_confidence: built 1924, completed 1925 (Ennis House Foundation; Wikipedia). Coordinate corrected to 34.1161/-118.2928 at 2607 Glendower Avenue, about 800 m north of the pool's pin. 'Largest' is confirmed; 'last' is disputed, Wikipedia recording the construction order of the textile-block houses as contested, with some accounts placing the Freeman House after Ennis. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: High on a ridge below Griffith Park he builds the Ennis house for Charles and Mabel Ennis, the largest of the textile-block houses: perforated and patterned blocks stacked into something that reads from the road as a Maya platform set down on a Los Angeles hillside. It is the last of the four by most accounts and not by all of them, the order of the Freeman and Ennis houses being contested. The blocks will keep failing and the house will keep being rescued for the next ninety years.
suggested_refs: The Ennis House, 2607 Glendower Avenue, Los Angeles

stops.name: Spring Green, the second fire
stops.date_confidence: 20 April 1925 attested. The cause is contradicted inside the pool and is left contradicted: chronology says crossed telephone wires, geography states a lightning-caused electrical fire as fact, and the verification pass says neither is established, that Wright's own account puts the origin near a telephone in his bedroom, and that scholars only theorise the storm surge. Also corrected: the fire destroyed the living quarters of Taliesin II, not a 'bungalow'. Coordinate corrected to 43.1411/-90.0706. Iovanna born 3 December 1925.
stops.campa: The living quarters of Taliesin burn a second time, on the twentieth of April, taking the rooms and the Japanese print collection with them. Wright rebuilds on the same stone and calls the result Taliesin III. What started it is not settled: his own account puts the origin near a telephone in his bedroom, one line of the record says crossed telephone wires, and scholars have theorised an electrical surge off an approaching storm. Olgivanna Lazovich is living with him by now. Their daughter Iovanna is born in December.
suggested_refs: The burned living quarters of Taliesin II and the lost Japanese print collection

stops.name: Chandler, the Ocatillo camp
stops.date_confidence: [R] in the pool and stays [R] (Secrest; Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation archives). The camp, the angle-of-the-mountains construction, the unbuilt San Marcos-in-the-Desert resort and the later dismantling for lumber are traditional accounts rather than documented ones. Coordinate 33.2861/-111.8256, near present-day Chandler. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: South-east of Phoenix, on a low rise of desert, he throws up a camp for himself and his draftsmen in a few weeks: boards set at the angle of the mountains behind them, white canvas flaps stretched over for roof and wall, scarlet triangles on the doors. He calls it Ocatillo, after the plant. It exists to draw one job, a resort called San Marcos-in-the-Desert, which the crash that autumn kills before a wall goes up. The camp is left standing and the boards go for firewood.
suggested_refs: The Ocatillo Desert Camp near Chandler, Arizona, and the unbuilt San Marcos-in-the-Desert

stops.name: Spring Green, the Fellowship and the Disappearing City
stops.date_confidence: the Fellowship founded 1932 with 23 initial students, and The Disappearing City published 1932, both attested (Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation; Wikipedia). Location flagged: the pool gives three different pins for the Fellowship and its own note says it operated out of the Hillside buildings, so the Hillside coordinate is used. The Froebel-to-Fuller link is stated in felix_adler.journey.json; Feynman's Froebel kindergarten is attested in richard_feynman.journey.json; neither file names Wright, so the extension to him is reconstruction, resting on Brosterman's Inventing Kindergarten as cited at QUEUE.md line 280. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: With no commissions to speak of he opens a school. Twenty-three apprentices pay to come to Spring Green, work the farm, cook, quarry stone, rebuild the Hillside buildings, and draft. The same year he publishes The Disappearing City, proposing Broadacre: an acre a family, no city at all, everything reached by car. Friedrich Froebel's Gifts run through Felix Adler's kindergartens to Buckminster Fuller and to Richard Feynman; Wright is teaching out of the same box of blocks he was handed at nine.
stops.quote: I doubt if there is anything in the world uglier than a Midwestern city.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright, address at Evanston, Illinois, 8 August 1954
suggested_refs: The Taliesin Fellowship at the Hillside buildings, Spring Green
The Disappearing City (1932) and the Broadacre City model

stops.name: Mill Run, Fallingwater over Bear Run
stops.date_confidence: designed 1935, construction concluding 1937, at about $155,000 including an $8,000 architect's fee, attested (Wikipedia). The pool gives the span as 1935-1939 in geography and 1935-1937 in chronology; both are defensible, one covering the whole complex and one the house, and neither is chosen. The dispute with Kaufmann's consulting engineers over the cantilever is standard in the literature and is not separately attested in the verified pool. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Edgar Kaufmann, a Pittsburgh department store owner, has a weekend camp on Bear Run and expects a house looking at the waterfall. Wright puts the house on top of it: reinforced concrete trays cantilevered off a stone core, so that the water runs out from under the living room and is heard everywhere and seen from nowhere. Kaufmann's engineers say it will come down. Wright has the extra steel taken out. It costs about a hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars, of which eight thousand is his fee.
stops.quote: I believe in God, only I spell it "Nature".
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright, as quoted in Quote magazine, 14 August 1966; the issue itself was not located and the attribution is posthumous
suggested_refs: Fallingwater, Bear Run, Mill Run, Pennsylvania

stops.name: Racine, the Johnson Wax Building
stops.date_confidence: hired late July 1936, construction from September 1936, completed April 1939, all confirmed (S.C. Johnson corporate archives via Secrest; Wikipedia, 'Johnson Wax Headquarters'). Day defaulted. Coordinate corrected by about 1.6 km to 42.7136/-87.7908, 1525 Howe Street. The column load test and the sixty-ton figure are standard in the literature and are not attested in the verified pool; treat them as traditional.
stops.campa: Herbert Johnson hires him in late July to build an office for the wax company at Racine, and gets a windowless brick building lit through Pyrex tubes, with a great workroom carried on slender concrete columns that flare at the top into lily pads. The state building inspector refuses to permit them. Wright has one column cast, stands it in the yard, and has sandbags piled on it until it is carrying many times what is asked of it. The building is completed in April 1939.
stops.quote: Architecture is the triumph of Human Imagination over materials, methods, and men, to put man into possession of his own Earth.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright, c. 1930; carried by the Canadian Centre for Architecture with no work named, and appearing on Wikiquote only as an uncited caption
suggested_refs: The Johnson Wax Administration Building, 1525 Howe Street, Racine, and its dendriform columns

stops.name: Madison, the first Usonian house
stops.date_confidence: the Herbert and Katherine Jacobs First House, completed 1937 in Madison, is regarded as the first fully realised Usonian house (Wikipedia). The five thousand dollar figure is standard in the literature and is not attested in the verified pool. GAP: the pool carries no coordinate for the house, so the pin is Madison generally rather than the building on Toepfer Avenue. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: For Herbert Jacobs, a Madison newspaperman, and his wife Katherine he builds a house on the western edge of town for about five thousand dollars: one storey, flat roof, no basement, no attic, no garage but a carport, the kitchen a workspace open to the living room, heating pipes run in the concrete floor slab, plywood and brick walls the same on both faces. He calls the type Usonian, after Usonia, his word for the United States. It is the first of them fully realised.
suggested_refs: The Herbert and Katherine Jacobs First House, Madison, Wisconsin, 1937

stops.name: Scottsdale, Taliesin West in the Sonoran desert
stops.date_confidence: the site was acquired in 1937; Wikipedia dates the start of construction to 1938, and the pool's claim that Wright begins building in 1937 is corrected accordingly. Coordinate corrected to 33.6064/-111.8453; the pool's 33.6098/-111.8483 is off, and its address element 'Cave Creek Rd' is wrong, Taliesin West standing at 12621 N. Frank Lloyd Wright Boulevard, with Cave Creek Road an unrelated Phoenix arterial some 15 km west. The acreage and the seasonal migration are standard in the institutional literature and are not attested in the verified pool. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He buys a stretch of Sonoran desert below the McDowell mountains and begins, the following year, a winter camp that never quite stops being a camp: desert masonry of local rock set into concrete forms, redwood trusses, canvas stretched overhead for a roof that lets the light through. The Fellowship drives out every autumn and back every spring, the whole school moving twice a year. He is seventy. He has twenty-two years and a large part of his built work still in front of him.

stops.name: Lakeland, Florida Southern College
stops.date_confidence: commission 1938, when Ludd Spivey approached Wright; the first building, Annie Pfeiffer Chapel, completed 1941, with the construction span running 1941-1958; 12 of 18 planned buildings built, the largest single-site collection of Wright's work, all attested (Wikipedia). The pool's chronology dates the commission 1941, conflating it with the first completion, and is corrected. That students cast blocks and worked on construction is standard in the college's own account and is not attested in the verified pool. GAP: no coordinate in the pool, so the pin is the campus. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Ludd Spivey, president of a small Methodist college at Lakeland with almost no money, writes to ask for a campus. Wright designs eighteen buildings and a system of covered walkways to tie them together, and the students cast the blocks and put up a good deal of it themselves. The chapel is finished in 1941 and the last of the twelve in 1958. It is the largest collection of his work on any single site anywhere, and it stands in an orange grove in central Florida.
suggested_refs: Florida Southern College, Lakeland, and the Annie Pfeiffer Chapel of 1941

stops.name: New York, the Guggenheim begun
stops.date_confidence: design begun 1943 and occupying Wright until his death (Wikipedia; Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation). Hilla Rebay's commissioning letter and the counts of schemes and drawings are standard in the museum's institutional history and are not attested in the verified pool; treat the numbers as traditional. Coordinate 40.783/-73.959, inherited byte-identical from hilma_af_klint.journey.json and cecilia_vicuna.journey.json. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Hilla Rebay writes on behalf of Solomon Guggenheim asking for a museum for non-objective painting, a temple for it, she says, and a monument. Wright answers with one continuous ramp coiling upward inside a widening drum, so that a visitor rides to the top and walks down through the collection without ever turning back on himself. He is seventy-six. The drawings will go through scheme after scheme and hundreds of sheets, and the building will not open in his lifetime.
stops.quote: The mother art is architecture. Without an architecture of our own we have no soul of our own civilization.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Frank Lloyd Wright; no page citation located
suggested_refs: The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1071 Fifth Avenue, New York
Hilla Rebay's correspondence commissioning the museum

stops.name: Madison, the Unitarian Meeting House
stops.date_confidence: designed 1947, completed 1951 (First Unitarian Society of Madison documentation); month and day defaulted. That the Lloyd Jones family were among the society's founders, and that congregants hauled the stone themselves, are standard in the congregation's own account and are not attested in the verified pool. Coordinate 43.0761/-89.4442, 900 University Bay Drive.
stops.campa: The First Unitarian Society of Madison, the congregation his mother's family helped found, asks for a meeting house. He gives them a prow: a copper roof folding up to a point of glass above the pulpit, and stone hauled in from a quarry thirty miles off by the congregation in their own trucks. It stands a few minutes from the university he left without a degree, and a short drive from the street the family were living on when his father walked out. He is eighty when he designs it.
stops.quote: Every great architect is -- necessarily -- a great poet.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright, The Future of Architecture (1953)
suggested_refs: The First Unitarian Society Meeting House, 900 University Bay Drive, Madison
sources: First Unitarian Society of Madison documentation

stops.name: Bartlesville, Price Tower
stops.date_confidence: built 1952-1956, his only realised skyscraper, on a taproot foundation with a tree-like structural core (Price Tower Arts Center; Wikipedia). The nineteen storeys, the small original brief, the mixed apartment and office plan and the size of the town are standard in the building's own literature and are not attested in the verified pool. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Harold Price, who runs a pipeline construction company in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, asks for a small building for his engineers. Wright talks him into a tower. It goes up on a central shaft with the floors cantilevered off it like branches off a trunk, copper louvres outside, apartments on one quarter of each floor and offices on the rest. It is the only skyscraper he ever gets built, out of fifty years of drawing them, and it stands in a town of some thirty thousand people.
stops.quote: If it keeps up, man will atrophy all his limbs but the push-button finger.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright, quoted in Newsweek, 16 May 1955, from a lecture at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston
suggested_refs: Price Tower, Sixth and Dewey, Bartlesville, Oklahoma

stops.name: Phoenix, the death after surgery
stops.date_confidence: died 9 April 1959 at Phoenix, aged 91, following surgery (Wikipedia; Secrest; New York Times obituary, 10 April 1959). The hospital, St Joseph's, is the standard attribution but could not be confirmed from a fetchable source in this pass; the coordinate 33.4795/-112.0872 is St Joseph's at 350 W Thomas Road, correcting the pool's pin about 800 m south-east. The pool says 'five months before the Guggenheim opens' at one entry and six at two others; 9 April to 21 October is just over six, and six is used. The built-work counts are traditional and are not attested here.
stops.campa: He is taken into hospital at Phoenix with abdominal pain, operated on, and appears to be recovering. On the ninth of April he dies, ninety-one years old, six months before the Guggenheim opens and with its drawings still being argued over with the New York building department. He has been designing buildings for seventy-two years. Several hundred of them are standing, and a large share of everything he built he built after his seventieth birthday.
suggested_refs: St Joseph's Hospital, Phoenix, the standard but unconfirmed place of death
New York Times obituary, 10 April 1959

stops.name: Spring Green, buried at Unity Chapel
stops.date_confidence: burial in the Lloyd Jones family graveyard beside Unity Chapel in April 1959, confirmed (contemporary press; Wisconsin Historical Society; Wikipedia, 'Unity Chapel'). Coordinate corrected to 43.1325/-90.0614; the pool's two entries give 43.1394/-90.0669 and 43.144/-90.076, roughly 0.9 and 1.7 km off. The day of burial was not reached, so the month is attested and the day defaulted. The 1880s date for the chapel building is traditional.
stops.campa: They bring him back to the Valley and put him in the Lloyd Jones ground beside Unity Chapel, the small shingled building his family raised in the 1880s, near his mother and near Mamah Borthwick, whom he had buried in the same ground forty-five years before, on the hillside his Welsh grandparents took up when they came over. The chapel is a few minutes' walk from Taliesin and a few more from the school his aunts ran. A stone is set with his name on it. It holds for twenty-six years.
suggested_refs: Unity Chapel and the Lloyd Jones family cemetery, Wyoming Township, Iowa County, Wisconsin

stops.name: New York, the Guggenheim opens
stops.date_confidence: opened 21 October 1959, six months after Wright's death (Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation). The af Klint exhibition (opening 12 October 2018, over six hundred thousand visitors, the most-visited show in the museum's sixty-year history) and the Vicuna installation (from 27 May 2022) are attested in hilma_af_klint.journey.json and cecilia_vicuna.journey.json, both of which name Wright's spiral directly. The critical reception of the building on opening is traditional and is not attested in the verified pool. Pin inherited byte-identical from those two files.
stops.campa: The museum opens on the twenty-first of October, six months after his death, and the critics spend a decade complaining that the building eats the paintings. Fifty-nine years later Hilma af Klint's Ten Largest go up the ramp and six hundred thousand people come to see them, the best-attended show the place has ever had; she had asked in 1906 for a spiral temple and been given a rented studio. In 2022 Cecilia Vicuna hangs Spin Spin Triangulene in the same well, sixty-three years after the ramp was finished.
stops.quote: The physician can bury his mistakes, but the architect can only advise his clients to plant vines.
stops.quote_source: Frank Lloyd Wright, quoted in New York Times Magazine, 4 October 1953
suggested_refs: Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 2018-2019
Cecilia Vicuna, Spin Spin Triangulene, Guggenheim, 2022

stops.name: Scottsdale, the exhumation
stops.date_confidence: the 1985 exhumation, cremation and relocation to Taliesin West at Olgivanna's direction, against the wishes of Wisconsin family members and over objections from the Wisconsin Legislature, are confirmed (Wikipedia, 'Unity Chapel' and 'Taliesin West'; Secrest; Huxtable, Frank Lloyd Wright: A Life). Coordinate corrected to 33.6064/-111.8453; the pool's afterlife pin was about 2.9 km off. That the Wisconsin headstone remains in place over an empty grave is reconstruction, from Building Conservancy site notes and local press, unconfirmed against a primary source. The characterisation of the act as body-snatching is interpretive tradition. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Olgivanna Lloyd Wright dies, having left instructions. Wright's body is taken up out of the Wisconsin grave, cremated, and the ashes mixed with hers and set in a memorial garden at Taliesin West, on the desert ground he bought at seventy. The Wisconsin family are not told beforehand and object afterward; the state legislature objects too, and nothing comes of either. Local accounts say the headstone stays where it was, over nothing, and no primary record was reached to confirm it.

The empty marked grave at Unity Chapel, Wisconsin

stops.name: New York, the archive leaves Taliesin West
stops.date_confidence: the joint transfer of the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation archives to the Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library at Columbia and to the Museum of Modern Art was announced in 2012 (Columbia / MoMA joint announcement). The contents are not itemised in the verified pool, so no counts are given. Coordinate 40.8075/-73.9626, Avery Library. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation gives up the archive in 2012. Drawings, correspondence, models and photographs go jointly to the Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library at Columbia and to the Museum of Modern Art, out of the vaults at Taliesin West where they had sat since his death in 1959. The papers and the buildings are now in separate custody in separate states. Anyone who wants to check what he actually drew comes to Morningside Heights to do it.

stops.name: Spring Green, eight buildings inscribed as one
stops.date_confidence: inscribed July 2019 (UNESCO World Heritage List, official inscription record); day defaulted. The verified pool names only four of the eight components, Fallingwater, the Guggenheim, Taliesin and Taliesin West, and the other four are not enumerated here. The site is distributed and has no single coordinate; pinned at Taliesin, 43.1411/-90.0706, as one of the eight.
stops.campa: UNESCO inscribes eight of his buildings as a single World Heritage Site under the name The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright. Fallingwater is in it, and the Guggenheim, and Taliesin, and Taliesin West; the record reached here names only those four of the eight. It is the first modern architecture in the United States to be listed. The eight are treated as one property, so the site has no single address, and this stop stands at Taliesin, the hub of the group.
